items.topic: WHO My 5 Moments — hand hygiene before touching a patient
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: According to the WHO “My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene,” when must the nurse clean hands to protect the client from germs carried on the nurse’s hands from the health-care area?

options.text: Before touching the patient when approaching them (e.g., before taking a pulse or assisting with personal care)
Only at the start of the shift, then gloves replace further hand hygiene
Only after leaving the facility at the end of the day
Only if the nurse notices visible dirt, never before clean contact

rationales.A: Correct. WHO Moment 1: clean hands before touching a patient when approaching them to protect against colonization/exogenous infection. OpenStax Fundamentals links timely hand hygiene before direct patient contact to WHO’s Five Moments.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene; moments apply throughout care.
rationales.C: Incorrect. End-of-day hygiene does not replace point-of-care moments.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Moment 1 applies before patient contact even when hands are not visibly soiled (ABHR is typically appropriate then).

sources.title: Hand Hygiene: Why, How & When?
sources.section: Your 5 Moments — Before touching a patient
sources.evidence: Moment 1: clean hands before touching a patient when approaching him/her; protects patient from harmful germs on HCW hands; applies before pulse/BP/personal care.

sources.title: 10.2 Asepsis and PPE
sources.evidence: Hand hygiene before direct contact with a patient; references WHO Five Moments of Hand Hygiene.

items.topic: NGN matrix — WHO My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene indications
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: Using the WHO “My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene,” indicate whether each action requires hand hygiene at that moment (Indicated) or does not match a required moment as stated (Not indicated).

rows.text: Clean hands before touching the patient when approaching them
Clean hands immediately before a clean/aseptic procedure (e.g., accessing an invasive device)
Clean hands after body-fluid exposure risk and after glove removal
Skip hand hygiene after touching the patient if gloves were worn the whole time
Skip hand hygiene after touching patient surroundings because the patient was not touched

rationales.R1: Indicated. WHO Moment 1 — before touching a patient.
rationales.R2: Indicated. WHO Moment 2 — before clean/aseptic procedure.
rationales.R3: Indicated. WHO Moment 3 — after body-fluid exposure risk (and after glove removal).
rationales.R4: Not indicated. WHO notes hand hygiene is required in the indications whether or not gloves are used; Moment 4 is after touching a patient.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. WHO Moment 5 requires hand hygiene after touching patient surroundings even without touching the patient.

sources.title: Hand Hygiene: Why, How & When?
sources.evidence: Lists Moments 1–5; note that HH must be performed in all indications regardless of glove use; Moment 5 after surroundings without patient contact.

sources.title: 10.2 Asepsis and PPE
sources.evidence: HH before direct contact; after contact with skin; before/after glove use; references WHO Five Moments.

items.topic: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene — HH before donning and after removal
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A nurse plans to wear gloves for anticipated contact with body fluids. Which statement best reflects infection-prevention guidance about gloves and hand hygiene?

options.text: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene; clean hands before donning gloves and after removing them
Once gloves are on, hand hygiene is unnecessary for the rest of the shift
Hand hygiene is needed only before gloves, never after removal
Gloves replace hand hygiene when caring for every client on Contact Precautions

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene; perform HH before donning gloves and always after removing gloves. WHO: HH indications apply whether or not gloves are used.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Moments continue throughout care; gloves do not eliminate HH.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC requires cleaning hands after glove removal because dirty gloves can soil hands.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Contact Precautions still require HH; gloves are additive, not a replacement.

Clean hands after removing gloves
Change gloves and clean hands when moving from a soiled body site to a clean body site on the same patient
Rely on gloves alone and skip hand hygiene for the entire shift
Continue wearing the same gloves from one patient to the next without changing

rationales.R2: Indicated. CDC: always clean hands after glove removal.

items.topic: Total hip replacement — avoid hip flexion >90°, crossing legs, and use abduction pillow as directed
items.stem: A nurse teaches an older adult after total hip replacement about positioning to reduce dislocation risk. Which instruction is most appropriate when postoperative hip precautions are ordered?

options.text: Avoid bending the hip more than about 90°, do not cross the legs (avoid adduction), and use an abduction pillow in bed as directed
Cross the operative leg over the other leg frequently to stretch the joint
Sit in low soft chairs so the knees are higher than the hips
Bend forward to tie shoes immediately after surgery without adaptive equipment

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills: after THR avoid adduction/crossing legs, use abduction pillow, do not bend more than 90° forward, use raised seats so knees stay lower than hips. AAOS: special precautions when sitting/bending/sleeping to prevent dislocation; home planning includes raised seating and aids to avoid excessive bending.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Crossing legs adducts the hip and increases dislocation risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Low soft chairs promote excessive flexion; raised seating keeps knees lower than hips.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Excessive bending is avoided; adaptive equipment is recommended.

sources.title: 25.2 Physical Assessment
sources.section: Take Action: Postoperative Total Hip Replacement Patient
sources.evidence: Avoid twisting/adduction; do not cross legs; abduction pillow; do not bend more than 90°; raised seats with knees lower than hips.

sources.title: Total Hip Replacement
sources.evidence: Special precautions when sitting, bending, or sleeping to prevent dislocation (often ~6 weeks; approach-specific). Home planning: raised toilet/seat so knees remain lower than hips; dressing aids to avoid excessive bending.

items.topic: Hospital universal fall precautions — call light within reach and nonslip footwear
items.stem: Which nursing action best reflects universal hospital fall precautions for an older adult?

options.text: Keep the call bell within reach, ensure the patient can use it, and provide nonslip footwear when out of bed
Place the call bell across the room so the patient walks for exercise before calling
Encourage walking in socks without footwear to improve “grip” on linoleum
Keep personal items out of reach so the patient must stand unassisted to retrieve them

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills (AHRQ-aligned universal fall precautions): call bell within reach and demonstrated; nonslip well-fitting footwear. AHRQ PSNet: universal precautions include placing call light and necessary items within reach.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Call light must remain within reach.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Nonslip footwear is recommended; socks alone increase slip risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Personal possessions should be within safe reach.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Professional Boundaries and Nurse-Client Relationships practice standard
items.topic: CNO boundaries — avoid inappropriately sharing personal information (boundary crossing)
items.stem: During a therapeutic interaction, a nurse begins sharing detailed personal life problems with a client to “feel closer.” What is the best analysis of this action under Ontario professional standards?

options.text: It risks a boundary crossing; nurses should avoid inappropriately sharing personal information and keep the focus on the client’s needs
It is required by CNO as mandatory personal disclosure with every client
It is always appropriate because any personal sharing strengthens professional boundaries
It is acceptable if the nurse posts the same details on social media about the client

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: boundary crossings may include inappropriately sharing personal information; nurses must clarify/reinforce therapeutic boundaries. OpenStax: maintain professional boundaries—general talk may be OK, but avoid specific personal details; keep rapport without crossing boundaries.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Personal disclosure is not a mandatory CNO requirement.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Inappropriate personal sharing can create role confusion and harm.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Discussing/posting client-related content on social media violates privacy/boundaries.

sources.title: Professional Boundaries and Nurse-Client Relationships
sources.evidence: Boundary crossing examples may include preferential attention, socializing, or inappropriately sharing personal information; reflect and re-establish boundaries.

sources.title: 6.1 Nurse-Client Relationship
sources.evidence: May talk about family in a general way but would not provide specific personal details; maintain professional boundaries while building rapport.

items.stem: Complete the statement about maintaining a therapeutic nurse–client relationship in Ontario.

ngn.template: Inappropriately sharing personal information with a client can be a {B1}. After recognizing a boundary breach, the nurse should {B2}.

B2.text: reflect, take action to protect the client, and re-establish appropriate boundaries

invite the client to become a personal friend on social media

items.topic: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist — confirm sponge/instrument/needle counts before patient leaves OR
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: During the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist “sign out,” before the patient leaves the operating room, which confirmation is the circulating/scrub nurse expected to make to help prevent retained surgical items?

options.text: Verbally confirm that instrument, sponge, and needle counts are complete (and alert the team if counts do not reconcile)
Skip counts if the case finished quickly, because retained items are impossible in short procedures
Assume counts are correct without verbal confirmation once the surgeon starts closing
Discard sponges outside the room before the final count to save time

rationales.A: Correct. WHO SSC implementation: nurse verbally confirms completion of instrument, sponge and needle counts before the patient leaves the OR; if counts do not reconcile, alert the team. AHRQ: unintended retention of a foreign object after surgery is a serious reportable “never event.”
rationales.B: Incorrect. Retained items are uncommon but persistent; counts are required for eligible cases.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Verbal confirmation is an explicit checklist step.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Items should not be removed from the OR until counts are complete/reconciled.

items.jurisdiction_note: Health Canada AUVI-Q prescribing/patient information aligns with MedlinePlus epinephrine autoinjector site teaching
items.topic: Epinephrine autoinjector — inject into middle outer thigh; not buttocks, digits, or IV
items.stem: A client with a history of severe allergy asks where to use an epinephrine autoinjector in an emergency. Which teaching is correct?

options.text: Inject into the middle of the outer thigh (anterolateral thigh); do not inject into the buttocks, fingers/hands/feet, or a vein
Inject into a fingertip for fastest absorption
Inject into the buttock as the preferred adult site
Give only as an intravenous push at home without emergency follow-up

rationales.A: Correct. Health Canada AUVI-Q: inject into middle outer/anterolateral thigh; do not inject IV, buttocks, or digits/hands/feet. MedlinePlus: inject only in the middle of the outer side of the thigh; do not inject buttocks, fingers, hands, feet, or into a vein.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Digit injection risks severe vasoconstriction/ischemia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Buttock injection is specifically contraindicated for autoinjectors.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Autoinjectors are IM/SC into the thigh and emergency care must still be sought.

sources.title: AUVI-Q prescribing information

sources.evidence: Inject IM or SC into anterolateral aspect of the thigh; ONLY outer thigh; do not inject IV, buttocks, digits/hands/feet.

B1.text: middle of the outer thigh (anterolateral thigh), through clothing if needed
forearm vein with a home IV start

B2.text: seek emergency medical care right away even if symptoms improve

inject a second dose into a fingertip prophylactically
discard teaching and reuse the same device on another person later that day

rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Not for home IV administration.

rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Emergency evaluation is required after anaphylaxis treatment.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Devices are single-use for the prescribed patient.
